# Problem 1

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

In the NOAA dataset, there are `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables total. Using skimr::skim, the dataset includes 1 date variable, 3 numeric variables (e.g. prcp, snow, and snwd), and 3 character variables (e.g. ID, tmax, tmin). Skimr::skim also shows that although there are no missing observations for date, there is substantial missing data in the dataset. Prcp has 145,838 and snow has 381,221 missing observations, with snwd having a higher amount of missing data at 591786. Tmax and tmin have the greatest amount of missing data reaching the 1134000's.

```{r}
noaa_df = 
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep="-") |>
  mutate(
  year = as.numeric(year),
  month = as.numeric(month),
  tmax = as.numeric (tmax)/10,
  tmin = as.numeric (tmin)/10,
  prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```

Date was separated into year, month, and day. Year, month, tmax, and tmin were all converted into numeric variables, and tmax, tmin, and prcp were divided by 10, convertng tenths of degrees C to degrees C and tenths of mm to mm.

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  count(snow) |>
  mutate(snow_rank = min_rank(desc(n))) |>
  filter(snow_rank <= 10) |>
  arrange(snow_rank)
```

For snowfall, the most commonly observed values seem to be 0 and NA. This would mean that there are many days where there is no snowfall or the data is simply missing. The third and fourth highest rank values are 25 mm with 31022 observations, and 13 mm with 23095 observations.

```{r}
noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1,7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean (tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  ggplot (aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .5) + 
  facet_grid(. ~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (C)"
  )
```

Observing the two-panel plot, July's weather is warmer than January by about ~25 degrees C or so, and January's temperature fluctuated more throughout the years. The most notable outlier for January is a single scratch line moving downwards to -13ish degrees C around 1982. In contrast, the most notable outlier for July is a scratch line reaching down to 14ish degrees C in 1988 and moving back upwards afterwards.

```{r}

library(patchwork)

tmax_tmin_p = 
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot (aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() + 
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(
    x = "Minimum temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (C)"  
  )

snow_p = 
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

tmax_tmin_p + snow_p
```

The tmax vs tmin plot shows that when minimum temperature increases, maximum temperature increases as well. At about (12, 22), the highest number of weather stations fall in a range between 12 and 22 degrees C. 

Examining the snowfall graph, mediation snowfall has been consistently 25 mm from 1981 to 2010. In the 1900's, the interquartile range for snowfall was consistently between 12 mm and 51 mm, with some exceptions like in 1998. However, since 2006,the interquartile range seemed to fluctuate more with more outliers towards the higher end of the snowfall range.

# Problem 2
```{r}
accel_df = 
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_accel.csv")|>
  janitor::clean_names()

covar_df = 
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    filter(age >=21) |>
      drop_na(sex, age, education) |>
      mutate(
        sex = case_match(
          sex,
          1 ~ "male",
          2 ~ "female"
      ),
      sex = as.factor(sex),
      education = case_match(
        education,
        1 ~"Less than high school",
        2 ~"High school equivalent",
        3 ~"More than high school"
      ),
      education = factor(
        education,
        levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent","More than high school")
      ))
      
accelerometer_df = 
  inner_join(accel_df, covar_df, by = "seqn") 

accel_long = 
 accelerometer_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

accelerometer_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

accelerometer_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  facet_grid(. ~education) + 
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  )
```

Looking at the frequency table, it seems that while the less than high school education group and more than high school group had balanced female and male groups, there were more males than females in the high school equivalent group. 

Among those with less than a high school education, females had a higher median age than men and a slightly smaller interquartile range. When males and females had high school equivalent education, females had a higher median age, as well as a higher interquartile range than men. Men had a higher median age than women among those who had more than a high school education.

```{r}
accel_activity = 
  accel_long |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

accel_activity |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Among those with less than high school education, total activity over the day seems to decrease with age, with a little spike around 50-60 years age. Among those with equivalent high school education, total activity over the day rises with age until 40, dipping until 70, and stagnating afterwards. Among those with more than high school education, total activity over the day stagnates until 50 years old, and then drops slowly in a parabolic manner.

```{r}
accel_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(.~ education) + 
  labs(
    x = "Minute",
    y = "Average MMIS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Among all education groups as well as between men and women, average MMIS seems to decrease at 250 minutes, until increasing to 15 at 7500 minutes, and dipping back down in a parabolic manner afterwards.  Among those with less than high school education, females had a lower dip at 250 minutes compared to men. In contrast, females had a higher peak among those with equivalent high school education and an event higher average activity among those with more than high school education

# Problem 3

```{r}
jan20_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/jan_2020.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

jan24_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/jan_2024.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

july20_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/july_2020.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

july24_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/july_2024.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )

citibike_df = 
  bind_rows(jan20_df, jan24_df, july20_df, july24_df) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January","July")),
  weekdays = factor(
    weekdays,
    levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday","Saturday","Sunday")
  ))
```

Citi Bike is a bike sharing system in New York City; riders can rent pedal-powered or electric bikes from starting stations and return them to another station at their destination. Introduced in 2013, the system is immensely popular and expanded rapidly. Riders who use this system often may become “members” with lower rental rates.

This zip file contains data on rides taken on the NYC Citi Bike system. Files contain 1% of all rides with a total duration less than 4 hours in each of four months. Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset.

```{r}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.

```{r}
citi_df|>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  drop_na(start_station_name) |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  mutate(
    station_rank = min_rank(desc(n))
  ) |>
  filter(station_rank <= 5) |>
  arrange(station_rank) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.

```{r}
citi_df|>
  group_by(year, month, weekday) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = mediation_duration, color = month, group = month)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(. ~year) + 
  labs(
    x = "Day",
    y = "Median ride duration",
    color = "Month"
  )
```

Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.

```{r}
citi_df|>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
   ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(rideable_type ~ month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration"
  )
```

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.
